Literature review

Abstract

Modern life increasingly requires participation in more and more digital systems, and the relationship with technology that we are building is increasingly unsustainable. People are increasingly feeling as if they've lost control, relegated to passengers of their own lives. Gen Z has been most affected by this, with only 14% feeling comfortable with their screen time[^1]. Yet many report being unable to change; 80% cite FOMO and lack of motivation as the biggest factors keeping them on their phones, 28% are actively struggling to cut back, and 12% have given up trying entirely[^1]. This review examines the neuroscience of boredom, its connection to the brain's default mode network, the consequences of its elimination by modern technology, and why existing solutions have failed. I propose that the answer is not in restricting phone use, but in reclaiming boredom itself through a purposefully boring "micro-gadget" built on the basis of neuroscience research.

Background

The Neuroscience of Boredom and the Default Mode Network

When you have nothing to do, no task to focus on, no notification to check, instead of shutting, your brain activates a set of interconnected structures known as the default mode network (DMN). The DMN drives some of the most important cognitive processes we have: introspection, self-reflection, autobiographical memory, and long-term life planning[^2]. Researchers describe the DMN as the brain's system for making sense of who you are and where you're going in life.

The self-reflection hypothesis of the DMN suggests that during periods of rest, the network facilitates reflection on past experiences and future possibilities, allowing you to imagine and plan possible scenarios for your life[^3]. The DMN also plays a critical role in creative thinking. A 2024 study published in Brain found that creativity can be reliably predicted by the frequency of switches between the DMN and the executive control network (ECN). This suggests that the interplay between undirected thought and focused cognition is the foundation of creative problem-solving[^4]. Boredom is not the 'absence of thought' its to as today, instead it is the foundation wherein our most meaningful thinking can be built.

The Elimination of Boredom

Despite the importance of the DMN, modern technology has found a way to shut it off almost entirely. Apps like TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts have effectively "cured" boredom by providing infinite on-demand stimulation via scrolling short form content. The moment one feels even a flicker of discomfort from having nothing to do, one of these apps can be opened in a matter of to fill the void. The result of this is staggering and frankly horrifying: 83% of respondents in a recent survey noted that they had spent zero time "relaxing or thinking" in the past 24 hours[^1]. For an entire generation, the DMN is barely getting the chance to activate.

This is not simply a matter of preference or personal choice. Research suggests that we find the experience of directionless thought deeply uncomfortable[^2]. In a landmark 2014 study published in Science, Wilson et al. left participants alone in a room for 6 to 15 minutes with nothing to do but think. 67% of male participants and 25% of female participants chose to administer painful electric shocks to themselves rather than sit with their own thoughts, participants who had previously stated they would pay money to avoid being shocked again[^5]. Boredom is for so many people intolerable. And smartphones have provided the perfect escape.

The scale of phone dependency among Gen Z is hard to overstate. 68% of Gen Z respondents report feeling anxious when separated from their smartphones, compared to only 37% of Baby Boomers[^6]. 63% check their phones within five minutes of waking due to fear of missing out[^6]. Smartphones prove to be the hardest device for Gen Z to put down, with 61% ranking them as the most difficult to reduce usage on[^1]. The black box in everyone's pocket has become a crutch against the discomfort of an idle mind, and the consequences are becoming evident.

The Consequences

Gen Z is facing a mental health crisis that researchers are increasingly linking to the elimination of boredom and the rise of constant digital stimulation. A 2023 Gallup survey found that almost half (47%) of Gen Z individuals ages 12 to 26 often or always feel anxious, and more than one in five (22%) often or always feel depressed[^7]. A systematic review of 50 studies covering approximately 1.9 million adolescents found that excessive screen time is associated with mental health problems, with smartphone use during weekdays particularly correlated with diminished well-being.[^8] Corroborating this, adolescents with seven or more hours of daily screen time were found to be twice as likely to experience depression or anxiety compared to those with lower usage[^6].

The connection between screen time and a lack of purpose is where it gets really concerning. A Harvard report found that half of Gen Z young adults say their mental health is negatively affected by not knowing what to do with their lives, and nearly three in five (58%) reported lacking meaning or purpose in their lives within the past month[^9]. Arthur Brooks, writing in the Harvard Business Review, argues that this is not a coincidence. He contends that the avoidance of boredom through constant device use creates a "doom loop of meaning," where introspection brought on by the DMN, which historically helped people figure out their purpose, is being systematically prevented[^2]. We're the generation with the most access to information and entertainment, yet also the generation with the least sense of what we want to do with our lives, and the neuroscience suggests these two facts are directly related.

Existing Responses and Why They Fall Short

The tech industry's response to the screen time crisis has been largely focused on restriction, be that; screen time tracking apps, app blockers, usage timers, and guilt-based notifications telling users they have exceeded their daily limit. These approaches have proven insufficient. Research has shown that screen time tracking alone has little effect on phone behavior six weeks after implementation[^10]. Default rules such as time limits and pre-scheduled downtime fail to exert sustainable influence because you don't perceive tangible negative consequences when you dismiss these nudges; you just tap through them[^10]. One study found that while design friction interventions like grayscale mode led to immediate reductions in screen time, they produced no measurable improvement in subjective well-being or academic performance, which raises the question of whether reducing screen time alone is even the right goal[^10].

Cal Newport, in his book Digital Minimalism, argues that willpower-based tips and screen time apps are fundamentally insufficient as the solutions they offer treats symptoms rather than the cause. What is needed, he writes, is "a full philosophy of technology use" that gives people a compelling reason to put their phones down, not just a barrier preventing them from picking them up[^11]. Every major solution on the market focuses on restriction, and restriction alone does not address the underlying FOMO and motivational problem that 80% of Gen Z identifies as the reason they can't stop[^1].

There is a growing movement of deliberately limited devices that represent a more promising direction. The Micro-journal project offers an open-source, open-hardware distraction-free writing device in the genre of writerDecks[^12]. The Xteink X4 is a 74-gram, wallet-sized e-ink reader that magnetically snaps onto the back of your phone via MagSafe; it has no touchscreen, no frontlight, no app store, and no internet connection, you sideload DRM-free EPUBs and that's it[^14]. One review argued that reading apps on phones fail because they compete with notifications and social feeds, so you end up doomscrolling instead of finishing that novel[^15]. The X4's magnetically attached to the thing you're trying to use less, it's always right there as an alternative. The Tangara is an open-source, open-hardware portable music player inspired by the iPod, built around an ESP32 with a capacitive touch wheel, 3.5mm jack, and Bluetooth[^16]. Its entire philosophy is about ownership and control. It lets you listen to music on a dedicated device separate from the one with the infinite scroll, decoupling one more activity from your phone's ecosystem of distractions.

These "boring gadgets" share a philosophy of doing less on purpose, and they're each solving real problems. The X4, Tangara and Micro-journal all address the idea that reading, music, and writing devices are also your doomscrolling and notifications device. But none of them are built around the neuroscience of why boredom itself matters. They replace specific phone activities with dedicated alternatives, which is incredibly valuable as a first step, but they don't actively create space for the kind of undirected thinking that the DMN requires. They give you something to do instead of scrolling; nothing gives you nothing to do, which is what the DMN actually needs. The gap remains: no existing device offers a compelling, neuroscience-grounded replacement that makes doing nothing feel worth doing.

Conclusions

  • Boredom is not something to be cured; it is essential to reclaim. The DMN requires space to operate and drives the introspection, creativity, and sense of purpose that Gen Z is increasingly missing.
  • The elimination of boredom through constant digital stimulation is directly linked to rising rates of depression, anxiety, and a pervasive lack of purpose among young Gen Z.
  • Restriction-based approaches to screen time, from apps to timers to nudges, have consistently failed because they do not address the underlying motivational and emotional drivers of phone dependency.
  • The gap in the market and in the research is a device that does not just limit technology use, but offers a neuroscience-grounded alternative that makes "doing nothing" feel worth doing.
